records.source: הִנָּ֨ךְ יָפָ֤ה רַעְיָתִי֙ הִנָּ֣ךְ יָפָ֔ה עֵינַ֣יִךְ יוֹנִ֔ים מִבַּ֖עַד לְצַמָּתֵ֑ךְ שַׂעְרֵךְ֙ כְּעֵ֣דֶר הָֽעִזִּ֔ים שֶׁגָּלְשׁ֖וּ מֵהַ֥ר גִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: Look, you [are] beautiful, my companion; look, you [are] beautiful; your eyes [are] doves behind your veil; your hair [is] like a flock of the goats that stream down from Mount Gilead.
pieces: How beautiful you are, my darling! How beautiful you are! \q Your eyes are doves \q seen through your veil. \q Your hair is like a flock of goats \q pouring down the slopes of Mount Gilead.

L.1: Oh, you [are] beautiful, my companion! Oh, you [are] beautiful! \q Your eyes [are] doves \q from behind your veil. \q Your hair [is] like a flock of goats \q that stream down from Mount Gilead.

R.1: My darling, you are so beautiful! So beautiful! \q Behind your veil your eyes are like doves. \q Your hair is like a flock of black goats \q running down the slopes of Mount Gilead.

decisions.choice: the man speaks (4:1-15)
decisions.reason: "You" is feminine and he calls her "my companion" (1:9). The first line repeats his praise of 1:15.

decisions.choice: a song in praise of her body (4:1-7)
decisions.reason: Here the man describes her from head to breast, comparing each part with something from the land around them. Such songs were part of ancient love poetry, and the Song has three of them (4:1-7; 5:10-16; 7:2-10). The comparisons are about color, shape, movement and worth, not about how things look side by side: hair is not goats, but it ripples like a flock moving down a hill.

decisions.choice: your veil
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here, in 4:3 and 6:7, and in Isaiah 47:2, where a woman removes it. It is probably a veil; some take it to mean her hair falling over her face.

decisions.choice: your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Gilead: long dark hair falling in waves
decisions.reason: The goats of the land are black. Seen from far off, a flock moving down a hillside ripples like long dark hair. Gilead is the hill country east of the Jordan, known for its rich pasture (Numbers 32:1; Micah 7:14). The verb occurs only here; it seems to mean to stream or leap down.
The opening praise is worded as in 1:15 at each level.

decisions.choice: black goats
decisions.reason: Readable says the goats are black, which is what makes them like her hair (m4).

records.heading: He praises her beauty

records.source: שִׁנַּ֨יִךְ֙ כְּעֵ֣דֶר הַקְּצוּב֔וֹת שֶׁעָל֖וּ מִן־הָרַחְצָ֑ה שֶׁכֻּלָּם֙ מַתְאִימ֔וֹת וְשַׁכֻּלָ֖ה אֵ֥ין בָּהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: Your teeth [are] like a flock of the shorn [ewes] that have come up from the washing, which all of them bear twins, and a bereaved one there is not among them.
pieces: Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn ewes \q that have come up from the washing; \q each one has its twin, \q and not one of them is missing.

L.2: Your teeth [are] like a flock of shorn [ewes] \q that have come up from the washing, \q all of which bear twins, \q and not one among them has lost [its young].

R.2: Your teeth are as white as sheep that have just been sheared \q and washed in the stream. \q They are all in pairs, \q and not one of them is missing.

decisions.choice: teeth like shorn, washed sheep: white and clean
decisions.reason: Newly sheared and washed sheep are as white as they will ever be.

decisions.choice: all bear twins, none bereaved: an even, complete set
decisions.reason: Each ewe has a twin lamb and none has lost one: her teeth are matched in pairs, and not one is missing, a mark of health and beauty in a time when many lost teeth young.

decisions.choice: as white as sheep ... washed
decisions.reason: Readable says what the comparison means (m1, m2).

records.source: כְּח֤וּט הַשָּׁנִי֙ שִׂפְתֹתַ֔יִךְ וּמִדְבָּרֵ֖יךְ נָאוֶ֑ה כְּפֶ֤לַח הָֽרִמּוֹן֙ רַקָּתֵ֔ךְ מִבַּ֖עַד לְצַמָּתֵֽךְ׃
records.gloss: Like a thread of the scarlet [are] your lips, and your mouth [is] lovely; like a slice of the pomegranate [is] your temple behind your veil.
pieces: Your lips are like a scarlet thread, \q and your mouth is lovely; \q your cheeks behind your veil \q are like halves of a pomegranate.

L.3: Like a thread of scarlet [are] your lips, \q and your mouth [is] lovely; \q like a half of a pomegranate [is] your cheek \q behind your veil.

R.3: Your lips are like a thin red ribbon. \q Your mouth is lovely. \q Your cheeks behind your veil \q are as rosy as a pomegranate cut in half.

decisions.choice: lips like a scarlet thread: fine and red
decisions.reason: Scarlet thread was dyed bright red (Joshua 2:18); her lips are fine in shape and red in color.

decisions.choice: your mouth
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here. It comes from the verb "to speak" and may mean the mouth, or the way she speaks.

decisions.choice: your cheek like half a pomegranate: round and blushing red
decisions.reason: A pomegranate is a round fruit with a hard red skin and many juicy red seeds inside; it was a sign of beauty and plenty (Exodus 28:33; Deuteronomy 8:8). A pomegranate cut open is rosy, and so is her face. The word for cheek may mean the temple, the side of the forehead.

decisions.choice: as rosy as a pomegranate cut in half
decisions.reason: Readable says what the comparison means (m3).

records.source: כְּמִגְדַּ֤ל דָּוִיד֙ צַוָּארֵ֔ךְ בָּנ֖וּי לְתַלְפִּיּ֑וֹת אֶ֤לֶף הַמָּגֵן֙ תָּל֣וּי עָלָ֔יו כֹּ֖ל שִׁלְטֵ֥י הַגִּבּוֹרִֽים׃
records.gloss: Like [the] tower of David [is] your neck, built in courses; a thousand the shields hung on it, all [the] shields of the warriors.
pieces: Your neck is like the tower of David, \q built in rows of stone; \q a thousand shields hang on it, \q all of them warriors' shields.

L.4: Like the tower of David [is] your neck, \q built in courses; \q a thousand shields hang on it, \q all the shields of the warriors.

R.4: Your neck is tall and straight like the tower of David, \q built with rows of stones. \q The jewelry around it is like a thousand shields \q hanging on the tower, the shields of brave soldiers.

decisions.choice: your neck like the tower of David: tall, upright and splendid
decisions.reason: No tower of David is known outside this verse; it was a tower of Jerusalem's defenses. Her neck is long and straight, and she holds her head high.

decisions.choice: in courses: in rows of stone
decisions.reason: The word occurs only here. It may mean built in layers or rows, or "for weapons", or "for trophies".

decisions.choice: a thousand shields hung on it: her necklaces
decisions.reason: Soldiers hung their shields on city towers for display (Ezekiel 27:10-11). Her necklace of many pieces, row on row, looks like the shields hung on a tower.

decisions.choice: tall and straight; The jewelry around it
decisions.reason: Readable says what the tower and the shields stand for (m1, m3).

records.source: שְׁנֵ֥י שָׁדַ֛יִךְ כִּשְׁנֵ֥י עֳפָרִ֖ים תְּאוֹמֵ֣י צְבִיָּ֑ה הָרוֹעִ֖ים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּֽים׃
records.gloss: Your two breasts [are] like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that feed among the lilies.
pieces: Your breasts are like two fawns, the twins of a gazelle, \q that feed among the lilies.

L.5: Your two breasts [are] like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, \q that graze among the lilies.

R.5: Your breasts are like two young deer, \q twin fawns of a gazelle feeding among the lilies.

decisions.choice: your breasts like twin fawns: soft, gentle, a matching pair
decisions.reason: Young gazelles are soft, graceful and lively, and twins are a perfect pair. The picture speaks of beauty that invites a gentle touch. It returns in 7:4.

decisions.choice: grazing among the lilies
decisions.reason: The fawns feed among lilies as the beloved does in 2:16; the flowers are part of the beauty of the scene (2:1).

records.source: עַ֤ד שֶׁיָּפ֨וּחַ֙ הַיּ֔וֹם וְנָ֖סוּ הַצְּלָלִ֑ים אֵ֤לֶךְ לִי֙ אֶל־הַ֣ר הַמּ֔וֹר וְאֶל־גִּבְעַ֖ת הַלְּבוֹנָֽה׃
records.gloss: Until that breathes the day and flee the shadows, I will go for myself to [the] mountain of the myrrh and to [the] hill of the frankincense.
pieces: Until the day breathes \q and the shadows flee, \q I will go to the mountain of myrrh \q and the hill of frankincense.

L.6: Until the day breathes \q and the shadows flee, \q I will go to the mountain of myrrh \q and to the hill of frankincense.

R.6: Until the day breathes \q and the shadows run away, \q I will go to the mountain of myrrh \q and the hill of frankincense.

decisions.choice: until the day breathes and the shadows flee: her words of 2:17
decisions.reason: The man repeats the woman's words of 2:17. There she called him to the mountains; here he says that he will go.

decisions.choice: the mountain of myrrh, the hill of frankincense: her own body
decisions.reason: After the praise of her breasts (4:5), the fragrant mountain and hill are a picture of her, perfumed with myrrh (1:13). He will go to her and stay through the night. The image is kept at every level.
The first two lines are worded as in 2:17 at each level.

records.source: כֻּלָּ֤ךְ יָפָה֙ רַעְיָתִ֔י וּמ֖וּם אֵ֥ין בָּֽךְ׃ס
records.gloss: All of you [is] beautiful, my companion, and a flaw there is not in you.
pieces: You are beautiful in every way, my darling; \q there is no flaw in you.

L.7: All of you [is] beautiful, my companion, \q and there is no flaw in you.

R.7: My darling, everything about you is beautiful. \q There is not a single flaw in you.

decisions.choice: flaw: a blemish
decisions.reason: The word is used of any defect or blemish (Leviticus 22:20; Deuteronomy 32:5; 2 Samuel 14:25). The praise that began in 4:1 ends by saying that she is perfect.

records.source: אִתִּ֤י מִלְּבָנוֹן֙ כַּלָּ֔ה אִתִּ֖י מִלְּבָנ֣וֹן תָּב֑וֹאִי תָּשׁ֣וּרִי׀מֵרֹ֣אשׁ אֲמָנָ֗ה מֵרֹ֤אשׁ שְׂנִיר֙ וְחֶרְמ֔וֹן מִמְּעֹנ֣וֹת אֲרָי֔וֹת מֵֽהַרְרֵ֖י נְמֵרִֽים׃
records.gloss: With me from Lebanon, bride, with me from Lebanon come; come down from [the] peak of Amana, from [the] top of Senir and Hermon, from [the] dens of lions, from [the] mountains of leopards.
pieces: With me from Lebanon, my bride, \q come with me from Lebanon! \q Come down from the top of Amana, from the peaks of Senir and Hermon, \q from the dens of lions, \q from the mountains of the leopards.

L.8: With me from Lebanon, bride, \q with me from Lebanon come! \q Come down from the peak of Amana, from the top of Senir and Hermon, \q from the dens of lions, \q from the mountains of leopards.

R.8: My bride, come with me from Lebanon! \q Come with me from Lebanon! \q Come down from the top of Amana, from the tops of Senir and Hermon, \q from where the lions have their dens \q and the leopards live in the mountains.

decisions.choice: bride: a young woman about to marry or newly married
decisions.reason: The word (kallah) is used of a bride and of a son's wife (Genesis 38:11; Jeremiah 2:32). He calls her "bride" six times in 4:8-5:1, and only there.

decisions.choice: Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon: the high mountains of the north
decisions.reason: Hermon is the highest mountain in the north of the land; Senir is another name for it or for part of its range (Deuteronomy 3:9; 1 Chronicles 5:23). Amana seems to be a peak of the range east of Lebanon, where the river Abana (2 Kings 5:12) rises.

decisions.choice: the dens of lions, the mountains of leopards: far away and out of reach
decisions.reason: Wild animals lived in these remote heights. He pictures her as far from him, in a place of danger and wonder, and calls her to come down to him.

decisions.choice: come down: or "look down"
decisions.reason: The verb may mean to travel or come down, or to look down from the heights.

decisions.choice: my bride
decisions.reason: Hebrew says only "bride" when calling to her; Balanced and Readable add "my", as English does in direct address.

records.heading: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride

records.source: לִבַּבְתִּ֖נִי אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּ֑ה לִבַּבְתִּ֨ינִי֙ בְּאַחַ֣ת מֵעֵינַ֔יִךְ בְּאַחַ֥ד עֲנָ֖ק מִצַּוְּרֹנָֽיִךְ׃
records.gloss: You have taken my heart, my sister, bride; you have taken my heart with one of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklaces.
pieces: You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride; \q you have taken it with a single glance of your eyes, \q with a single jewel of your necklace.

L.9: You have captured my heart, my sister, bride; \q you have captured my heart with one of your eyes, \q with one jewel of your necklace.

R.9: You have stolen my heart, my bride, dear as a sister. \q You stole it with one look from your eyes, \q with one jewel of your necklace.

decisions.choice: you have captured my heart
alternatives: you have made my heart beat fast
decisions.reason: The verb is made from the word for "heart" and occurs only here. It probably means "you have taken my heart"; it could also mean "you have made my heart beat fast".

decisions.choice: my sister, bride: a name of love
decisions.reason: "Sister" is a word of closeness and affection, as lovers in the love songs of the ancient Near East call each other "sister" and "brother" (compare 8:1). It does not mean that she is his sister by birth. With "bride" it says she is both his dearest companion and the one he will marry. The pair is used in 4:9-12 and 5:1.

decisions.choice: one of your eyes: one look from you
decisions.reason: A single glance is enough to overcome him.

decisions.choice: my bride, dear as a sister
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "my sister" (m2), so that the reader does not think of a real sister.

records.source: מַה־יָּפ֥וּ דֹדַ֖יִךְ אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּ֑ה מַה־טֹּ֤בוּ דֹדַ֨יִךְ֙ מִיַּ֔יִן וְרֵ֥יחַ שְׁמָנַ֖יִךְ מִכָּל־בְּשָׂמִֽים׃
records.gloss: How beautiful [is] your lovemaking, my sister, bride; how much better [is] your lovemaking than wine, and [the] fragrance of your oils than all spices!
pieces: How lovely your love is, my sister, my bride! \q Your love is so much better than wine, \q and the scent of your perfumes than any spice!

L.10: How beautiful [is] your lovemaking, my sister, bride! \q How much better [is] your lovemaking than wine, \q and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!

R.10: How beautiful your love is, my bride, dear as a sister! \q Your love is more delightful than wine. \q Your perfume smells sweeter than any spice.

decisions.choice: he answers her words of 1:2-3
decisions.reason: She said that his lovemaking was better than wine and his oils fragrant (1:2-3); he now says the same of her.

decisions.choice: lovemaking
love

records.source: נֹ֛פֶת תִּטֹּ֥פְנָה שִׂפְתוֹתַ֖יִךְ כַּלָּ֑ה דְּבַ֤שׁ וְחָלָב֙ תַּ֣חַת לְשׁוֹנֵ֔ךְ וְרֵ֥יחַ שַׂלְמֹתַ֖יִךְ כְּרֵ֥יחַ לְבָנֽוֹן׃ס
records.gloss: Honey from the comb drip your lips, bride; honey and milk [are] under your tongue, and [the] fragrance of your garments [is] like [the] fragrance of Lebanon.
pieces: Your lips drip with honey, my bride; \q honey and milk are under your tongue, \q and the scent of your clothes is like the scent of Lebanon.

L.11: Honey from the comb your lips drip, bride; \q honey and milk [are] under your tongue, \q and the scent of your garments [is] like the scent of Lebanon.

R.11: My bride, your lips are as sweet as honey. \q Honey and milk are under your tongue. \q Your clothes smell like the cedar forests of Lebanon.

decisions.choice: honey and milk: the sweetness of her kisses and her words
decisions.reason: Honey dripping from the comb was the sweetest thing known (Psalm 19:11; Proverbs 24:13). Her lips and tongue are sweet in her kisses and in what she says (Proverbs 5:3; 16:24). Milk and honey also recall the good land (Exodus 3:8).

decisions.choice: the fragrance of Lebanon: the scent of its cedar forests
decisions.reason: Lebanon's forests of cedar and other resinous trees filled the air with a strong, clean scent (Hosea 14:7).

decisions.choice: the cedar forests of Lebanon
decisions.reason: Readable says what gives Lebanon its scent (m2).

records.source: גַּ֥ן׀נָע֖וּל אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּ֑ה גַּ֥ל נָע֖וּל מַעְיָ֥ן חָתֽוּם׃
records.gloss: A garden locked [is] my sister, bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.
pieces: My sister, my bride, is a garden locked up, \q a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.

L.12: A garden locked [is] my sister, bride, \q a spring locked, a fountain sealed.

R.12: My bride, dear as a sister, you are like a garden with a locked gate, \q like a spring that is closed off, a fountain that is sealed.

decisions.choice: a locked garden, a sealed spring: she belongs to no one else
decisions.reason: Private gardens and springs were walled and sealed so that only the owner could enter or draw water. The pictures say that she has kept herself for him alone. A spring or fountain is also a picture of a wife's love (Proverbs 5:15-18). The images are kept at every level.

decisions.choice: a spring
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text has the word for a spring or pool (gal). Many Hebrew manuscripts and some ancient versions read "garden" (gan) again, a difference of one letter: "a garden locked, a garden locked, a fountain sealed".

decisions.choice: you are like a garden with a locked gate
decisions.reason: Readable speaks to her and adds "like" and "gate" to make the picture clear.

records.heading: A garden locked, a fountain sealed

records.source: שְׁלָחַ֨יִךְ֙ פַּרְדֵּ֣ס רִמּוֹנִ֔ים עִ֖ם פְּרִ֣י מְגָדִ֑ים כְּפָרִ֖ים עִם־נְרָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: Your shoots [are] an orchard of pomegranates with fruit of choice things, henna with nard,
pieces: Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates \q with the choicest fruits, \q henna and nard,

L.13: Your shoots [are] an orchard of pomegranates \q with choice fruits, \q henna with nard,

R.13: Your garden is a park of pomegranate trees \q with the best fruits, \q henna and nard,

decisions.choice: your shoots: what grows from her garden
decisions.reason: The word means what is sent out: shoots or branches of plants, or perhaps channels of water. The garden of 4:12 is now in full growth.

decisions.choice: orchard: an enclosed park
decisions.reason: The word (pardes) is borrowed from Persian, where it means a walled park; it is used also in Ecclesiastes 2:5 and Nehemiah 2:8. The Greek word from which "paradise" comes goes back to it.

decisions.choice: pomegranates, henna and nard: a garden of every delight
decisions.reason: Pomegranates (4:3), henna (1:14) and nard (1:12) begin a list of the finest fruits and spices. Several of them grew only in far countries, so no real garden held them all: this garden is a picture of her as every delight together.

decisions.choice: Your garden
decisions.reason: Readable names the garden of 4:12 instead of its shoots, to keep the picture clear.

records.source: נֵ֣רְדְּ׀וְכַרְכֹּ֗ם קָנֶה֙ וְקִנָּמ֔וֹן עִ֖ם כָּל־עֲצֵ֣י לְבוֹנָ֑ה מֹ֚ר וַאֲהָל֔וֹת עִ֖ם כָּל־רָאשֵׁ֥י בְשָׂמִֽים׃
records.gloss: nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all [the] chief spices.
pieces: nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, \q with every tree of frankincense, \q myrrh and aloes, \q and all the finest spices.

L.14: nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, \q with all [kinds of] trees of frankincense, \q myrrh and aloes, \q with all the finest spices.

R.14: nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, \q every kind of tree that gives frankincense, \q myrrh and aloes, \q and all the best spices.

decisions.choice: saffron, calamus, cinnamon
decisions.reason: Saffron is the bright yellow spice and dye made from a crocus flower (named only here). Calamus is a sweet-smelling cane or reed brought from far away (Exodus 30:23; Jeremiah 6:20). Cinnamon is the fragrant bark of a tree of South Asia (Exodus 30:23; Proverbs 7:17).

decisions.choice: frankincense, myrrh and aloes
decisions.reason: Frankincense and myrrh are resins (3:6; 1:13). Aloes here is a fragrant wood from Asia, not the aloe plant (Psalm 45:9; Proverbs 7:17).

records.source: מַעְיַ֣ן גַּנִּ֔ים בְּאֵ֖ר מַ֣יִם חַיִּ֑ים וְנֹזְלִ֖ים מִן־לְבָנֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: A fountain of gardens, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.
pieces: You are a fountain for gardens, \q a well of living water, \q streams that flow down from Lebanon.

L.15: A fountain of gardens, \q a well of living water, \q and streams flowing from Lebanon.

R.15: You are a spring that waters gardens, \q a well of fresh water, \q a stream that flows down from Lebanon.

decisions.choice: the man goes on speaking
decisions.reason: The sentence has no verb or pronoun; it continues his description of her as a garden. Some read this verse as the woman's reply, but she speaks clearly only in 4:16.

decisions.choice: living water: fresh running water
decisions.reason: Water from a spring or a running stream, not stored in a cistern (Genesis 26:19; Jeremiah 2:13). The sealed fountain of 4:12 now flows freely.

decisions.choice: streams from Lebanon: cold, clear water from the snows
decisions.reason: Streams fed by the snow of the Lebanon range run cold and clear all year (Jeremiah 18:14).

decisions.choice: You are
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "you are", which the context implies.

decisions.choice: a well of fresh water
decisions.reason: Readable says what "living water" means (m2).

records.source: ע֤וּרִי צָפוֹן֙ וּב֣וֹאִי תֵימָ֔ן הָפִ֥יחִי גַנִּ֖י יִזְּל֣וּ בְשָׂמָ֑יו יָבֹ֤א דוֹדִי֙ לְגַנּ֔וֹ וְיֹאכַ֖ל פְּרִ֥י מְגָדָֽיו׃
records.gloss: Awake, north wind, and come, south wind; blow on my garden; let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden and eat its choice fruits.
pieces: Wake up, north wind; come, south wind! \q Blow on my garden and let its fragrance drift out. \q Let my beloved come into his garden \q and taste its choice fruits.

L.16: Awake, north wind, and come, south wind! \q Blow on my garden; let its spices flow. \q Let my beloved come into his garden \q and eat its choice fruits.

R.16: North wind, wake up! South wind, come! \q Blow on my garden, so that its sweet smells spread. \q Let my love come into his garden \q and eat its best fruits.

decisions.choice: the woman answers
alternatives: the man speaks 4:16a and the woman 4:16b
decisions.reason: "Let my beloved come" can only be the woman. The first half of the verse may be hers too, calling the winds to spread the scent of her garden; it may also be the man, still speaking of the garden.

decisions.choice: north wind and south wind: let the scent spread
decisions.reason: The north wind is cool and the south wind warm (Job 37:9, 17). Together they carry the scent of the garden; she wants it to reach him.

decisions.choice: my garden ... his garden: she gives herself to him
decisions.reason: She calls the garden "my garden" and then "his garden": what is hers she now gives to him. To come into the garden and eat its fruit is a picture of the lovers' union; the image is kept at every level.

decisions.choice: so that its sweet smells spread
decisions.reason: Readable says what "let its spices flow" means: the scent of the spices spreads.
